lesson.title: Hidden Shifts I: V → B
lesson.subtitle: The quiet family: geben↔give, über↔over, sieben↔seven, Biber↔beaver

hook.title: The Quiet Family
hook.content: Some shifts make noise — PF explodes, ch growls. The V→B family whispers. Where English kept an ancient v or f between vowels, German closed it into a b: give → geben, live → leben, love → lieben, over → über, seven → sieben, half → halb. The consonant simply shut its mouth. English spells the difference with v, German with b — one letter, one gesture, a whole family of the most intimate words in either language: giving, living, loving. German hid the family so well you never noticed it was the same word.

footnotes.title: The Beaver Test
footnotes.content: The animal names prove it is a law, not a coincidence: beaver ↔ Biber, liver ↔ Leber, calf ↔ Kalb, silver ↔ Silber. Four unrelated creatures and materials, one systematic consonant correspondence.

pattern.title: Swap v for b, Hear the Verb
pattern.content: The verbs: give → geben, live → leben, love → lieben (and believe → glauben — the be- and the lieve both shifted!), drive → treiben (you drilled this one in the ablaut gallery). The numbers and measures: seven → sieben, half → halb. The colors and materials: yellow → gelb (double shift — the y too!), silver → Silber, leaf → Laub (foliage). The preposition you already own: over → über. Every one of these obeys the same quiet law: English v/f between vowels, German b.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “German V is English V.” It is English F: Vater is father. The safe test is to read a German V as an F and see whether an English word appears. If nothing does, leave it alone.
pattern.linguist_note: The direction is counterintuitive: German looks like it 'added' a b, but actually Proto-Germanic had a bilabial fricative *β where English wrote v/f and High German closed it to the stop b. Neither language changed its word — they pronounced the same sound differently, then spelled their habits.

exercises.prompt: Match the quiet family — swap v for b. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: geben, leben, lieben, sieben, Das Buch ist lang, Das Glas ist voll, der Wein, das ist gelb, Wir können glauben
exercises.meaning: give; live; love; seven; The book is long; The glass is full; the wine; that is yellow; We can believe
exercises.explanation: The most intimate verbs in both languages are one word each — with the consonant shut quietly into b.

exercises.prompt: Before the new family, which familiar pair uses a different clue?
exercises.meaning: Recognize a familiar German word by choosing between earlier connection patterns.
exercises.explanation: Thank, thumb and brother use TH → D. Help → helfen uses P → F.

exercises.prompt: English 'believe' and German 'glauben' — why are they twins?
options: be- ↔ ge- and the lieve/laube root — both elements correspond
exercises.target_answer: be- ↔ ge- and the lieve/laube root — both elements correspond
exercises.explanation: The prefix pair and the v→b root both line up: two languages building the same word from the same parts.

exercises.prompt: What English metal is the twin of 'Silber'?
exercises.explanation: The v closed to b — the same law that made give/geben. Silver, Silber: one metal, one word.

exercises.idea: you're explaining why you stay: you live in Germany and you love it
cues: Two quiet-family verbs: leben (live) and lieben (love) — English v between vowels became b, and wir takes -en on both
exercises.target_answer: Wir leben in Deutschland und wir lieben es
exercises.meaning: We live in Germany and we love it
exercises.affirmation: You heard the English v hiding inside both b's — leben and lieben in one breath, the quiet family.

vocab_hints.note: es ↔ it — the twin pronoun from the negation lesson

exercises.explanation: Two quiet-family verbs in one sentence: leben and lieben — living and loving, both shifted v's.

summary.outcome: Recognize the V→B family across verbs, numbers, and materials.

use_example.german: Wir leben in Deutschland und wir lieben es.
use_example.english: We live in Germany and we love it.

summary.takeaway: English v/f between vowels is German b: give/geben, love/lieben, over/über, seven/sieben — the quiet family.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: geben's full dynasty — Gabe, vergeben, and the Perfekt forms gab and gegeben.

twist.prompt: Rainy week — walk it back: we live in Germany and we love it becomes ...and we do NOT love it.
twist.target_answer: Wir leben in Deutschland und wir lieben es nicht
twist.explanation: nicht closes the clause where the action dies — after the object it negates. Word for word: '...and we love it not.'

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

glauben.etymology_derivation: be- ↔ ge- & lieve ↔ lauben (v → b). Governs dative case.

über.context_translation: We are speaking about / over the book.

halb.context_translation: It is half past seven (halfway to eight).

silber.context_translation: The ring is made of silver.

gelb.etymology_derivation: Double shift: y → g and w/v → b (yellow → gelb).

kalb.context_phrase: Die Kuh hat ein kleines Kalb.
kalb.context_translation: The cow has a small calf.

treiben.shift_rule: D → T + V / F → B + Ablaut Vowels
treiben.context_translation: What are you up to / driving at today?
treiben.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and v → b.

menü.context_phrase: Ich bestelle das Menü mit Suppe.
menü.context_translation: I am ordering the set menu with soup.
menü.etymology_derivation: Menü — borrowed from French menu, the same word behind English menu; its computing sense later came in as a semantic loan from English. [wiktionary]

möbel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed in the 15th century from Middle French meuble, from Latin mobilis, meaning movable; English mobile comes from the same Latin adjective. [wiktionary]

birke.context_phrase: Die Birke hat eine weiße Rinde.
birke.etymology_derivation: From Old High German birka, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā. English birch is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

prozent.context_phrase: Die Miete steigt um fünf Prozent.
prozent.context_translation: The rent rises by five percent.
prozent.etymology_derivation: From Italian per cento, Latin for by the hundred — the page confirms the same construction as English percent. [wiktionary]

polizei.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa — the same city-word (Greek polis) behind English police. [wiktionary]

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant *β remained a fricative in English but closed to a stop in High German.
